Around 100,000 knee replacements are performed each year in the UK, most for osteoarthritis. It's one of the most successful operations in modern medicine, with over 95% of patients reporting significant pain relief. Here's what you need to know about the process in the UK.

Quick answer: Knee replacement is recommended when severe pain affects quality of life, non-surgical treatments fail, and X-rays show significant joint damage. Approximately 100,000 such operations are performed annually in the UK, mostly for osteoarthritis. Recovery typically involves 1-3 days in hospital, followed by physiotherapy. Most people return to light activities in 6-12 weeks, with maximum benefit achieved around 12 months.

When Is Knee Replacement Recommended?

Knee replacement is considered when:

  • Pain is severe and affecting your quality of life
  • Non-surgical treatments (exercise, weight loss, physiotherapy, injections) haven't provided sufficient relief
  • X-rays show significant joint damage
  • You have difficulty with daily activities like walking, climbing stairs, or sleeping

There's no strict age limit — suitability is based on need and overall health.

Types of Knee Replacement

  • Total knee replacement (TKR) — the entire joint surface is replaced. Most common type.
  • Partial (unicompartmental) knee replacement — only the damaged section is replaced. Smaller operation, faster recovery, but not suitable for everyone.
  • Revision surgery — replacing a worn-out previous replacement (less common).

NHS Waiting Times

Current NHS waiting times for knee replacement vary significantly by region:

  • England: average 6-12 months, some areas longer
  • Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland: similar variation
  • You can check hospital waiting times at nhs.uk
  • Remember: you have the right to choose your hospital in England

What to Expect

Before Surgery

  • Pre-assessment clinic — blood tests, ECG, general health check
  • "Prehab" exercises — strengthening exercises before surgery improve recovery
  • Optimise weight and stop smoking if applicable

The Operation

  • Usually under spinal anaesthetic (you're awake but numb from the waist down)
  • Takes approximately 1-2 hours
  • You'll usually stay in hospital for 1-3 days

Recovery Timeline

  • Weeks 1-2 — walking with crutches, starting physiotherapy exercises
  • Weeks 3-6 — increasing mobility, reducing crutch use
  • Weeks 6-12 — most people return to driving and light activities
  • 3-6 months — significant improvement in pain and function
  • 12 months — maximum benefit usually achieved

Physiotherapy After Surgery

Physiotherapy is crucial for a good outcome:

  • NHS physiotherapy is provided post-operatively
  • Exercises focus on regaining range of motion and strength
  • You'll be given a home exercise programme to follow daily
  • Consistency with exercises is the single biggest factor in recovery

Risks and Considerations

  • Infection risk: approximately 1-2%
  • Blood clot risk: reduced with medication and compression stockings
  • Implant lifespan: modern replacements last 20-25+ years
  • Stiffness: some people need manipulation under anaesthetic if the knee doesn't bend well

Knee replacement is a major decision. Discuss all your options with your orthopaedic surgeon, and remember that preparation and post-operative physiotherapy are key to the best outcomes.

Practical next steps for Knee Replacement for Arthritis – UK Guide

If you came here about Knee Replacement for Arthritis – UK Guide, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask community musculoskeletal services about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Working with NHS pathways

Most people start with GP care, community physiotherapy and self-management, with rheumatology involved when inflammatory disease is suspected or treatment needs escalate. Ask what monitoring blood tests or reviews you should expect, and who to contact between appointments if a flare escalates.

Work, rights and practical adjustments

Under the Equality Act 2010, employers in Great Britain should consider reasonable adjustments when arthritis has a substantial long-term effect. That can mean flexible hours, more breaks, seating, parking closer to the entrance, or software that reduces typing strain. Acas and Citizens Advice both publish plain-English guides you can take into a meeting.

Quick questions about Knee Replacement Arthritis Guide

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.
